snip.t: | Pleural fluid cytology | Is pleural effusion malignant? | Malignant mesothelial cells → mesothelioma; otherwise benign exudate in asbestosis |

| Lung cancer with obstructive pneumonia | Smoking history, weight loss, persistent localized infiltrate; sputum cytology or biopsy positive | Persistent mass on imaging, lack of systemic infection signs, may have hilar enlargement |

| Malignant pleural effusion | Known cancer or weight loss, unilateral, bloody or serosanguineous fluid, cytology positive, exudate | Positive malignant cells on cytology, often recurrent, may have pleural thickening on CT |
Cytology (malignant cells), culture and Gram stain, AFB and GeneXpert, ADA (adenosine deaminase) high in TB.

| Lung cancer (central) | New‑onset cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, smoking history, hoarseness | Imaging (CT) reveals mass; may cause obstructive pneumonitis but not diffuse rhonchi; sputum cytology may show malignant cells |
Bronchoscopy (central tumours), EBUS (nodes), CT-guided percutaneous biopsy (peripheral), pleural fluid cytology or biopsy, node biopsy.
Pleural fluid (diagnostic tap): appearance, protein, LDH and glucose, pH, cell count and differential, Gram stain, culture, AFB and GeneXpert, ADA, cytology.

qs.q: During a lecture on anterior pituitary cytology, a medical student is asked to identify the glycoprotein hormones produced by the gland. Which of the following is correctly classified as a pituitary glycoprotein hormone?
o: Somatostatin-14 produced by neuroendocrine cells of the hypothalamus
Adrenocorticotropic hormone secreted by anterior pituitary corticotrophs
Growth hormone releasing hormone secreted by hypothalamic arcuate neurons
Thyroid-stimulating hormone produced by the anterior pituitary gland
qs.e: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), along with FSH and LH, is a glycoprotein hormone produced by the anterior pituitary. ACTH is a peptide, and GHRH and somatostatin are hypothalamic regulatory peptides.

qs.q: A 62-year-old woman with a large recurrent pleural effusion undergoes thoracentesis, and initial fluid cytology is negative for malignant cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
qs.e: When initial fluid cytology is negative for malignancy, repeating the thoracentesis for cytology increases diagnostic yield before proceeding to more invasive tissue biopsy. Initiating empirical therapy without tissue diagnosis is not standard practice.
qs.s: Pleural Effusion: Light's Criteria, Fluid Analysis and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A 45‑year‑old woman has a 2‑cm firm, non‑tender breast mass that is suspicious on ultrasound. Which statement best explains why a core (Tru‑Cut) needle biopsy is preferred over fine‑needle aspiration cytology for tissue diagnosis?
o: It is performed without local anaesthesia.
It eliminates the risk of bleeding.
It provides histology and receptor status.
It allows evaluation of cystic lesions.
qs.e: Core biopsy yields tissue architecture, hormone‑receptor information, and can distinguish invasive from in‑situ disease, which FNAC cannot provide. The other statements describe advantages that are not true for core biopsy.
qs.s: Breast Lumps and Breast Cancer: Triple Assessment, Staging and: MCQs

qs.q: A patient undergoes staging laparoscopy prior to planned curative surgery for gastric cancer. What is the primary purpose of performing peritoneal washings for cytology during this procedure?
o: To detect microscopic peritoneal disease missed by CT
To sterilize the peritoneal cavity prior to resection
To measure the exact depth of muscularis invasion
To confirm the presence of a Krukenberg ovarian mass
qs.e: Staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings for cytology is performed before major surgery to detect occult peritoneal disease missed by cross-sectional CT imaging. It prevents unnecessary laparotomies in patients with stage M1 disease.
qs.s: Gastric Cancer: Presentation, Staging and Gastrectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman is found to have high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions on routine screening cytology. Integration of which viral genome into host chromosomes is the primary oncogenic driver in this condition?
qs.e: High-risk human papillomavirus types like 16 integrate into host DNA and produce E6/E7 oncoproteins that inactivate p53 and Rb. Herpes simplex virus causes transient lytic infections rather than cervical carcinogenesis.

qs.q: During the processing of an exfoliative cytology specimen, which immediate step is critical to prevent cellular degradation prior to staining and microscopic examination?
qs.e: Alcohol or methanol fixation is applied immediately after sample collection to prevent degradation before the slide is smeared and stained. Embedding and deparaffinisation are steps used in tissue processing for histology and immunohistochemistry rather than routine cytology smear preparation.
qs.s: Crash course part 3 chemical pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman undergoes a routine gynaecological screening programme where cells from her cervical transformation zone are scraped and stained. Which specific staining method is standard for this type of exfoliative cytology?
qs.e: The Papanicolaou (Pap) stain is the multi-chromatic stain used for gynaecological cytology to give excellent nuclear detail and stain cytoplasm in shades of pink, green, or orange. Giemsa stain is typically used for air-dried preparations like haematology and FNA smears.
qs.s: Crash course part 3 chemical pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A pathologist examines a sputum cytology specimen from a patient suspected of having a lung malignancy. Which specific type of lung cancer is most amenable to diagnosis via sputum cytology?
qs.e: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung sheds malignant cells into the airways, making it the lung cancer most amenable to detection via sputum cytology. Adenocarcinoma and other subtypes are often more peripheral and less reliably identified through expectorated sputum.

ai.title: Cytology in Clinical Pathology
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Cytology examines cells from body fluids or tissues to identify disease, especially malignancy and infection. In low‑resource settings it guides diagnosis when histology or advanced imaging are unavailable.

sections.p: Cytology is the microscopic study of individual cells or small clusters obtained by fine‑needle aspiration, body‑fluid tap, or brushings. It provides rapid, minimally invasive clues to infection, inflammation, or cancer.
b: Samples: pleural, peritoneal, pericardial fluid; FNAB of masses; urine, sputum, cervical brushings.
Key diagnostic criteria: cellular atypia, abnormal nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, mitoses, and specific infectious organisms.

sections.p: Cytology itself does not stage disease, but the presence of malignant cells in fluid (e.g., pleural) upgrades a cancer to stage IV (M1) in most solid‑tumour staging systems.
b: Positive malignant cytology = distant metastasis for lung, breast, ovarian, etc.
High cellularity with necrosis often indicates aggressive tumour.

sections.p: Cellular abnormalities arise from infection, inflammation, or neoplasia. In East African hospitals the most common etiologies are:
b: Tuberculosis (acid‑fast bacilli in pleural fluid, granulomatous inflammation).
Malignant mesothelioma or lung cancer (malignant mesothelial or epithelial cells).
Parasitic infections (Schistosoma eggs in peritoneal fluid).
HIV‑related opportunistic infections (CMV, Kaposi sarcoma cells).

sections.p: Patients present with the underlying disease: pleural effusion causing dyspnoea, ascites with abdominal distension, or a palpable mass. Cytology does not produce symptoms itself.
b: Unilateral bloody pleural fluid → suspect malignancy.
Exudative, lymphocyte‑rich fluid → TB or lymphoma.
Low glucose, low pH → empyema or malignant effusion.

sections.p: Cytology is performed on the same sample used for routine fluid analysis. When a microscope is unavailable, a basic stain (e.g., Giemsa) can still reveal key features.
b: If microscopy is unavailable, send the sample to a regional lab; meanwhile treat presumptively based on clinical picture.

t.a: Fluid appearance and biochemistry (protein, LDH, glucose, pH)
t.b: Distinguish transudate vs exudate; low glucose/pH suggests infection or malignancy.
Identify bacterial infection; negative culture with exudate raises TB or malignancy.
Detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis; positive result confirms TB pleuritis.
Detect malignant cells, parasites, or characteristic inflammatory patterns.
Allows immunocytochemistry for tumour typing when basic stains are inconclusive.

sections.p: Missing a malignant effusion delays cancer treatment; untreated empyema can cause sepsis and fibrothorax.
b: Rapidly increasing effusion with haemorrhage.
Persistent fever despite antibiotics.
New‑onset pleural thickening on chest X‑ray.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; cytology results guide specific therapy.
b: TB pleuritis – standard 6‑month anti‑TB regimen; avoid steroids unless severe inflammation.
Malignant effusion – therapeutic thoracentesis, pleurodesis (talc) if recurrent; systemic chemotherapy based on tumour type.
Empyema – broad‑spectrum antibiotics plus chest tube drainage; avoid fibrinolytics if tuberculous.
Parasitic ascites – praziquantel for schistosomiasis; supportive diuretics.

sections.p: Repeat cytology only if the clinical picture changes. Preventable causes include smoking cessation, TB control programs, and safe water to limit schistosomiasis.
b: Monitor fluid re‑accumulation with bedside ultrasound.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B to reduce liver‑cancer‑related effusions.

sections.p: Cytology findings can be mistaken for other fluid analyses.
b: Pleural fluid analysis alone (biochemistry) – does not identify cells.
Histopathology – requires tissue architecture, not just cells.

sections.p: False‑negative cytology is common when tumour cells are scant or when sampling is poor.
b: Low‑volume taps may miss malignant cells; repeat tap if suspicion remains.
Reactive mesothelial proliferation can mimic malignancy – use immunostains when possible.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden respiratory distress from massive effusion
Rapidly enlarging unilateral effusion with haemorrhage

faq.q: Can a negative cytology rule out cancer?
faq.a: No; repeat sampling or tissue biopsy is needed if clinical suspicion stays high.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of lymphocyte‑rich pleural effusion in East Africa?
Why is pleural fluid pH important?
faq.a: A pH <7.2 suggests infection or malignancy and predicts need for drainage.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with HIV presents with unilateral bloody pleural effusion. What is your next diagnostic step — answer: send fluid for cytology, AFB smear, and GeneXpert because TB and malignancy are both common.
How does Light’s criteria help you interpret a pleural tap — answer: it distinguishes exudate (protein ratio >0.5, LDH ratio >0.6, or pleural LDH >2/3 ULN), guiding further cytology.

A patient’s pleural fluid cytology is negative but imaging shows a peripheral lung mass. What should you do — answer: proceed to image‑guided needle biopsy or thoracoscopy, as cytology can miss peripheral tumours.
Why is talc pleurodesis preferred over repeated thoracentesis for recurrent malignant effusion — answer: it prevents re‑accumulation, reduces hospital visits, and improves quality of life.

What feature on cytology distinguishes malignant mesothelioma from reactive mesothelial cells — answer: atypical nuclei with prominent nucleoli, loss of uniformity, and increased mitoses; immunostains (e.g., calretinin) help confirm.

In a low‑resource clinic without a microscope, how would you manage a suspected tuberculous pleural effusion — answer: treat empirically with anti‑TB drugs after ruling out bacterial empyema, and arrange referral for later cytology if possible.
